notes.heading: Physical quantities and units
notes.body_md:
- A physical quantity is anything measurable; it is stated as a number times a unit.
- Fundamental (base) quantities are chosen independently; derived quantities are built from them.
- The SI system has seven base quantities: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol), luminous intensity (cd).
- Radian (plane angle) and steradian (solid angle) are supplementary/dimensionless units.
- Prefixes: milli = $10^{-3}$, micro = $10^{-6}$, nano = $10^{-9}$, kilo = $10^{3}$, mega = $10^{6}$, giga = $10^{9}$.

notes.heading: Measuring length, mass and time
notes.body_md:
- Small lengths: 1 angstrom = $10^{-10}$ m, 1 fermi = $10^{-15}$ m. Large: 1 light year = $9.46\times10^{15}$ m, 1 parsec is about $3.08\times10^{16}$ m.
- Indirect methods (parallax, triangulation) are used for distant or very small objects.
- Atomic mass unit: 1 u = $1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg.
- Time is measured with periodic phenomena; atomic clocks give the best precision.
- Orders of magnitude help compare scales, from the nucleus ($10^{-15}$ m) to the universe ($10^{26}$ m).

notes.heading: Accuracy, precision and errors
notes.body_md:
- Accuracy: closeness to the true value. Precision: closeness of repeated readings to each other.
- Systematic errors (instrument, personal, method) push results one way; random errors scatter results and are reduced by averaging.
- Least count error is the smallest division an instrument can read.
- Absolute error = |measured - mean|; mean absolute error is the average of these.
- Relative error = mean absolute error / mean value; percentage error = relative error x 100.

notes.heading: Combination of errors
notes.body_md:
- Sum or difference: absolute errors add, $\Delta Z=\Delta A+\Delta B$.
- Product or quotient: relative errors add, $\Delta Z/Z=\Delta A/A+\Delta B/B$.
- Power $Z=A^{p}B^{q}$: $\Delta Z/Z = p\,\Delta A/A + q\,\Delta B/B$ (the powers are used with positive sign).
- Worst case is assumed in school problems, so errors are always added.

notes.heading: Significant figures
notes.body_md:
- All non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant.
- Leading zeros are not significant ($0.0045$ has 2).
- Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant ($2.500$ has 4).
- In multiplication/division, the result keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor.
- In addition/subtraction, the result keeps as many decimal places as the least precise term.
- Scientific notation removes ambiguity in trailing zeros.

notes.heading: Dimensions of physical quantities
notes.body_md:
- Dimensions show how a quantity depends on M, L, T (and others) written as $[M^aL^bT^c]$.
- Examples: velocity $[LT^{-1}]$, acceleration $[LT^{-2}]$, force $[MLT^{-2}]$, work/energy $[ML^2T^{-2}]$, power $[ML^2T^{-3}]$, pressure $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$, density $[ML^{-3}]$.
- Pure numbers, angles, strain and trigonometric arguments are dimensionless.
- Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated.

notes.heading: Dimensional analysis and its limits
notes.body_md:
- Uses: (1) check the correctness of an equation, (2) convert units between systems, (3) derive relations between quantities.
- The principle of homogeneity: every term in a valid equation has the same dimensions.
- Limits: it cannot give dimensionless constants (such as $1/2$ or $2\pi$); it fails for relations involving sums of terms like $\sin$ or exponentials; it needs the right set of variables to be guessed.
- A dimensionally correct equation may still be physically wrong.

notes.heading: Instruments: vernier callipers and screw gauge
notes.body_md:
- Vernier least count = 1 main scale division - 1 vernier division.
- Screw gauge least count = pitch / number of circular scale divisions.
- Reading = main scale reading + (division coinciding x least count).
- Zero error must be subtracted: corrected reading = observed - zero error (with correct sign).
- Repeating readings at different places reduces random error.

pyqs.question: The dimensional formula of pressure is:
Using dimensions, check whether the equation $s=ut+\tfrac12 at^2$ is correct.
pyqs.solution_md: $[s]=L$. $[ut]=LT^{-1}\cdot T=L$. $[at^2]=LT^{-2}\cdot T^2=L$. Every term has dimension $L$, so the equation is dimensionally consistent (the factor 1/2 cannot be verified by this method).

pyqs.question: The mass and volume of a body are measured as $50.0\pm0.5$ g and $10.0\pm0.2$ cm$^3$. Find the density and its percentage error.
pyqs.solution_md:
Density $\rho=m/V=5.0$ g/cm$^3$.

$\dfrac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\dfrac{\Delta m}{m}+\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=\dfrac{0.5}{50}+\dfrac{0.2}{10}=0.01+0.02=0.03$.

Percentage error = 3%, i.e. $\rho=5.0\pm0.15$ g/cm$^3$.

pyqs.question: State the number of significant figures in (i) 0.04050 and (ii) $3.200\times10^{5}$.
pyqs.solution_md:
(i) Leading zeros are not counted; digits 4, 0, 5, 0 are significant (zero between and the trailing zero after the decimal point) so 4.
(ii) In 3.200 the trailing zeros after the decimal point are significant, so 4.

pyqs.question: Using dimensional analysis, derive an expression for the time period $T$ of a simple pendulum, assuming it depends on its mass $m$, length $l$ and acceleration due to gravity $g$. State one limitation of the method.
pyqs.solution_md:
Assume $T=k\,m^{a}l^{b}g^{c}$.

Dimensions: $[T]=T$, $[m]=M$, $[l]=L$, $[g]=LT^{-2}$.

$T^1 = M^{a}L^{b}(LT^{-2})^{c}=M^{a}L^{b+c}T^{-2c}$.

Comparing: $a=0$; $b+c=0$; $-2c=1\Rightarrow c=-\tfrac12,\ b=\tfrac12$.

Hence $T=k\sqrt{l/g}$, independent of mass.

Limitation: the dimensionless constant $k$ (actually $2\pi$) cannot be found by dimensional analysis.

pyqs.question: Which of the following has the dimensions of velocity? ($P$ = pressure, $\rho$ = density)
pyqs.solution_md: $P/\rho = ML^{-1}T^{-2}/ML^{-3}=L^2T^{-2}$, so $\sqrt{P/\rho}=LT^{-1}$, the dimension of velocity.

pyqs.question: $g$ is measured with a simple pendulum using $g=4\pi^2 l/T^2$. Length $l=1.00$ m is measured with error 1 mm and period $T=2.0$ s with error 0.02 s. Find the percentage error in $g$.
A screw gauge has pitch 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions. With no zero error, the main scale reads 2.5 mm and the 27th circular division coincides with the reference line. The reading is:
pyqs.solution_md:
Least count = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm.
Reading = 2.5 + 27 x 0.01 = 2.77 mm.

pyqs.question: A quantity is $Q=\dfrac{a^{2}\sqrt{b}}{c^{3}}$. The percentage errors in $a$, $b$, $c$ are 2%, 4% and 1%. Find the percentage error in $Q$.

Assertion (A): Dimensional analysis cannot give the numerical value of dimensionless constants in a formula.
Reason (R): Constants such as 1/2 and $2\pi$ have no dimensions, so they do not affect the dimensional equation.
options: (A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
(B) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
(C) A is true but R is false
(D) A is false but R is true
pyqs.solution_md: Dimensional equations compare powers of M, L, T only; a dimensionless number contributes nothing, so it cannot be determined. R is true and explains A.

notes.heading: Position, path length and displacement
notes.body_md:
- Motion is described relative to a reference frame; in 1-D we use a single axis with a chosen origin and positive direction.
- Path length is the total distance travelled (scalar, never negative or decreasing).
- Displacement is final position minus initial position (vector), so it can be zero or negative.
- Magnitude of displacement is at most the path length.

notes.heading: Speed and velocity
notes.body_md:
- Average speed = total path length / total time.
- Average velocity = displacement / time interval.
- Instantaneous velocity $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}$, the slope of the position-time graph.
- Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity.
- For a round trip, average velocity is zero but average speed is not.

notes.heading: Acceleration
notes.body_md:
- Average acceleration = change in velocity / time; instantaneous $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$.
- Speeding up occurs when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign, slowing down when opposite.
- A body can have zero velocity at an instant and non-zero acceleration (top of a vertical throw).
- Slope of the velocity-time graph gives acceleration.

notes.heading: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion
notes.body_md:
- $v=u+at$, $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$, $v^2=u^2+2as$.
- Distance in the $n$th second: $s_n=u+\tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$.
- These apply only for constant acceleration along a line, with signs taken from the chosen positive direction.
- They can be derived by integration: $a=dv/dt$ and $a=v\,dv/dx$.

notes.heading: Graphs of motion
notes.body_md:
- x-t graph: slope = velocity; a straight line means uniform velocity, a parabola means uniform acceleration.
- v-t graph: slope = acceleration; area under the graph = displacement.
- a-t graph: area under the graph = change in velocity.
- Area below the time axis counts as negative displacement, so total distance needs absolute areas.

notes.heading: Free fall
notes.body_md:
- Under gravity alone, every body has acceleration $g=9.8$ m/s$^2$ downward, independent of mass (air resistance neglected).
- Taking up as positive, use $a=-g$.
- Time to maximum height $=u/g$; maximum height $=u^2/2g$; time of flight (back to start) $=2u/g$.
- Speed at any height on the way up equals speed at the same height on the way down.

notes.heading: Relative velocity in one dimension
notes.body_md:
- Velocity of A relative to B: $v_{AB}=v_A-v_B$.
- Objects moving in the same direction: subtract speeds. Opposite directions: add speeds.
- Two objects approaching each other cover their separation at the relative speed.
- Always convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by $5/18$.

pyqs.question: A car moving at 20 m/s is braked with a uniform deceleration of 5 m/s$^2$. Find the stopping distance and the time taken.
A ball is thrown vertically upward with speed 29.4 m/s. Find the maximum height reached and the total time before it returns to the thrower's hand ($g=9.8$ m/s$^2$).
Starting from $a=v\,dv/dx$ for constant acceleration, derive $v^2=u^2+2as$.
pyqs.solution_md:
$a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}\Rightarrow a\,dx=v\,dv$.

Integrate from $x=0$ ($v=u$) to $x=s$ ($v=v$): $a\int_0^s dx=\int_u^v v\,dv$.

$as=\dfrac{v^2-u^2}{2}\Rightarrow v^2=u^2+2as$.

pyqs.question: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s$^2$ for 10 s, then moves at constant velocity for 20 s, and finally decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. Draw the v-t graph in words and find (i) the total distance, (ii) the average speed, (iii) the final deceleration.
pyqs.solution_md:
Stage 1: $v=at=20$ m/s; distance $=\tfrac12(2)(10)^2=100$ m.
Stage 2: constant 20 m/s for 20 s: $400$ m.
Stage 3: deceleration $=20/5=4$ m/s$^2$; distance $=\tfrac12(20)(5)=50$ m.

Total distance $=100+400+50=550$ m; total time $=35$ s.
Average speed $=550/35\approx15.7$ m/s.

Graph: a straight line rising from 0 to 20 m/s (0-10 s), flat (10-30 s), falling to 0 (30-35 s): a trapezium whose area is 550 m.

pyqs.question: The position of a particle is $x=2t^3-9t^2+12t$ (SI units). Its acceleration when it comes to momentary rest for the second time is:
pyqs.solution_md:
$v=6t^2-18t+12=0\Rightarrow t^2-3t+2=0\Rightarrow t=1,2$ s.
$a=12t-18$; at $t=2$ s, $a=6$ m/s$^2$.

pyqs.question: A stone dropped from rest from the top of a tower covers 44.1 m in the last second of its fall (this is exactly its $n$th second). Find the height of the tower ($g=9.8$ m/s$^2$).
Two trains, each 175 m long, move on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 72 km/h and 54 km/h. The time they take to completely cross each other is:
pyqs.solution_md:
Relative speed $=72+54=126$ km/h $=35$ m/s.
Distance to cover $=175+175=350$ m.
Time $=350/35=10$ s.

pyqs.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m/s from the top of a 25 m high building. Find the speed with which it hits the ground and the total time in air ($g=9.8$ m/s$^2$).

Assertion (A): A body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration at the same instant.
Reason (R): Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, not the value of velocity.
options: (A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
(B) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
(C) A is true but R is false
(D) A is false but R is true
pyqs.solution_md: At the top of a vertical throw $v=0$ but $a=g$. Since acceleration depends on how $v$ changes, R correctly explains A.

notes.heading: Scalars and vectors
notes.body_md:
- Scalars have magnitude only (mass, time, speed, energy); vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force).
- Equal vectors have the same magnitude and direction; a unit vector $\hat n$ has magnitude 1.
- A vector can be written as $\vec A=A_x\hat i+A_y\hat j$ with magnitude $\sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2}$.
- Multiplying by a scalar changes the magnitude (and reverses direction if the scalar is negative).

notes.heading: Vector addition and resolution
notes.body_md:
- Triangle and parallelogram laws give the resultant of two vectors.
- Magnitude $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors placed tail to tail.
- Direction: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}$ measured from $\vec A$.
- Resolution: $A_x=A\cos\theta$, $A_y=A\sin\theta$.
- Subtraction is addition of the negative vector.

notes.heading: Motion in a plane: velocity and acceleration
notes.body_md:
- Position vector $\vec r=x\hat i+y\hat j$; velocity $\vec v=d\vec r/dt$; acceleration $\vec a=d\vec v/dt$.
- With constant acceleration, x and y motions are independent and each follows the equations of motion.
- Velocity is always tangent to the path.

notes.heading: Projectile motion
notes.body_md:
- Horizontal motion: uniform velocity $u\cos\theta$. Vertical motion: uniformly accelerated with $a=-g$.
- Time of flight $T=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$; maximum height $H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$; range $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$.
- Range is maximum at $45^\circ$; angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ-\theta$ give the same range.
- Path is a parabola; speed is minimum at the top, where velocity is purely horizontal.
- Horizontal projection from height $h$: $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$.

notes.heading: Relative velocity in two dimensions
notes.body_md:
- $\vec v_{AB}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B$.
- River-boat problems: if the boat heads straight across, crossing time is $d/v_b$ (minimum) and drift is $v_r\,t$.
- To reach the point directly opposite, steer upstream at angle with $\sin\theta=v_r/v_b$.
- Rain-umbrella problems: tilt in the direction of the rain's velocity relative to the person.

notes.heading: Uniform circular motion
notes.body_md:
- Speed is constant but velocity changes direction, so there is acceleration directed to the centre.
- $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2r$ with $v=\omega r$ and $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi\nu$.
- Centripetal acceleration is perpendicular to velocity and does no work.
- In non-uniform circular motion there is also a tangential component of acceleration.

notes.heading: Dot and cross products
notes.body_md:
- Scalar product: $\vec A\cdot\vec B=AB\cos\theta$ (commutative); used in work and power.
- Vector product: $|\vec A\times\vec B|=AB\sin\theta$, direction by right-hand rule; anti-commutative; used in torque and angular momentum.
- Dot product is zero for perpendicular vectors; cross product is zero for parallel vectors.

pyqs.question: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at right angles. The magnitude of the resultant is:
Show that for a given speed the horizontal range of a projectile is maximum when the angle of projection is $45^\circ$.
pyqs.solution_md: $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$. For fixed $u$, $R$ is largest when $\sin2\theta=1$, i.e. $2\theta=90^\circ$, so $\theta=45^\circ$, and $R_{max}=u^2/g$.

pyqs.question: A projectile is fired at 50 m/s at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Find the time of flight, maximum height and range ($g=9.8$ m/s$^2$).
A particle moves on a circle of radius 2 m with a constant speed of 4 m/s. Find its centripetal acceleration, angular speed and time period.
Derive the expression $a=v^2/r$ for the centripetal acceleration of a particle in uniform circular motion. State its direction.
pyqs.solution_md:
Let the particle move from P to Q on a circle of radius $r$, turning through a small angle $\Delta\theta$ in time $\Delta t$ with speed $v$.

Velocity vectors at P and Q have equal magnitude $v$ and differ in direction by $\Delta\theta$. The triangle of $\vec v_P$, $\vec v_Q$ and $\Delta\vec v$ is similar to the triangle formed by the radii OP, OQ and chord PQ.

$\dfrac{|\Delta\vec v|}{v}=\dfrac{|\Delta\vec r|}{r}\Rightarrow|\Delta\vec v|=\dfrac{v}{r}|\Delta\vec r|$.

Dividing by $\Delta t$: $\dfrac{|\Delta\vec v|}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{v}{r}\dfrac{|\Delta\vec r|}{\Delta t}$. As $\Delta t\to0$, $|\Delta\vec r|/\Delta t\to v$.

Thus $a=v^2/r$. As $\Delta t\to0$, $\Delta\vec v$ becomes perpendicular to $\vec v$ and points towards the centre.

notes.heading: Aristotle's fallacy and Galileo's idea
notes.body_md:
- It is wrongly believed that a force is needed to keep a body moving; in fact a force is needed only to change its velocity.
- On a smooth surface a body keeps moving because the net force is zero.
- Friction and air drag are external forces that slow bodies in everyday life.

notes.heading: Newton's first law and inertia
notes.body_md:
- A body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by a net external force.
- Inertia is the property of resisting change in state; mass is its measure.
- Inertial frames are those in which the first law holds; frames accelerating relative to them are non-inertial.
- Examples: passengers jerk backward when a bus starts and forward when it stops suddenly.

notes.heading: Momentum and Newton's second law
notes.body_md:
- Linear momentum $\vec p=m\vec v$ (kg m/s).
- Net force equals rate of change of momentum: $\vec F=d\vec p/dt$, which is $m\vec a$ for constant mass.
- Force is a vector; components along each axis obey $F_x=ma_x$ etc.
- 1 newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s$^2$.

notes.heading: Impulse
notes.body_md:
- Impulse $\vec J=\vec F\,\Delta t=\Delta\vec p$ for a constant force; in general the area under the F-t graph.
- A large force acting for a very short time (bat hitting a ball) is an impulsive force.
- Increasing contact time reduces the force for the same change in momentum (cricketer pulling hands back).

notes.heading: Newton's third law and momentum conservation
notes.body_md:
- Forces between two bodies are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different bodies.
- Action and reaction never cancel because they act on different objects.
- If net external force is zero, total momentum is conserved: $m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2$.
- Applications: recoil of a gun, rocket propulsion, collisions.

notes.heading: Free body diagrams and common cases
notes.body_md:
- Draw only forces on the chosen body: weight, normal, tension, friction, applied force.
- Tension in a light string is the same throughout if the pulley is smooth and massless.
- Apparent weight in a lift: $N=m(g+a)$ going up with acceleration $a$, $N=m(g-a)$ when accelerating down; zero in free fall.
- Atwood machine and blocks connected by strings are solved by writing $F=ma$ for each block.

notes.heading: Friction
notes.body_md:
- Static friction adjusts to the applied force up to a maximum: $f_s\le\mu_sN$.
- Kinetic friction $f_k=\mu_kN$, nearly independent of speed and area; $\mu_k<\mu_s$ usually.
- Angle of friction $\lambda$ satisfies $\tan\lambda=\mu_s$; a block just begins to slide on an incline of angle of repose $\theta=\lambda$.
- Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.

notes.heading: Circular motion and banked roads
notes.body_md:
- Centripetal force $F=mv^2/r$ is provided by tension, friction, gravity or a component of normal force.
- On a flat road the maximum safe speed is $v_{max}=\sqrt{\mu_s rg}$.
- On a road banked at angle $\theta$ with no friction, the design speed satisfies $\tan\theta=v^2/rg$.
- Centripetal force is not an extra force; it is the net force towards the centre.

Momentum conservation (initially at rest): $0=m_bv_b-Mv_g$.
$v_g=\dfrac{0.05\times400}{4}=5$ m/s opposite to the bullet.

pyqs.question: A 10 kg block slides down a $30^\circ$ incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. Find its acceleration ($g=9.8$ m/s$^2$).

pyqs.solution_md:
On a banked road the horizontal component of the normal force $N\sin\theta$ supplies the centripetal force, so tyres need not rely on friction.

Vertical: $N\cos\theta=mg$. Horizontal: $N\sin\theta=mv^2/r$.

Dividing: $\tan\theta=v^2/(rg)$.

Numerically $\tan\theta=\dfrac{14^2}{50\times9.8}=\dfrac{196}{490}=0.4\Rightarrow\theta\approx21.8^\circ$.

notes.heading: Work done by a force
notes.body_md:
- Work $W=\vec F\cdot\vec d=Fd\cos\theta$ (joule); it is a scalar and can be positive, negative or zero.
- Zero work: force perpendicular to displacement (centripetal force, normal force on level motion) or zero displacement.
- Negative work: force opposite to displacement (friction, braking force).
- For a variable force $W=\int F\,dx$, the area under the F-x graph.

notes.heading: Kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem
notes.body_md:
- Kinetic energy $K=\tfrac12mv^2=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$; it is never negative.
- Work-energy theorem: the net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy, $W_{net}=K_f-K_i$.
- It holds for constant and variable forces and for all kinds of forces, including friction.

notes.heading: Potential energy and conservative forces
notes.body_md:
- A force is conservative if the work done depends only on end points (gravity, spring force) and is zero over a closed path.
- Gravitational potential energy near the Earth $U=mgh$ (relative to a chosen reference).
- Spring potential energy $U=\tfrac12kx^2$, where $x$ is the extension or compression.
- Friction and drag are non-conservative; they dissipate mechanical energy as heat.

notes.heading: Conservation of mechanical energy
notes.body_md:
- If only conservative forces do work, $K+U=$ constant.
- A freely falling body: loss of $U$ equals gain of $K$, $v=\sqrt{2gh}$.
- A pendulum or a block on a smooth curve exchanges $K$ and $U$ while total energy stays constant.
- With friction, the energy lost equals the work done against friction.

notes.heading: Spring and the work-energy method
notes.body_md:
- Spring force $F=-kx$ (Hooke's law) is restoring and conservative.
- Work done in stretching a spring from 0 to $x$: $\tfrac12kx^2$.
- A block released from a compressed spring on a smooth surface leaves with $v=x\sqrt{k/m}$.
- Total energy in a mass-spring system is $\tfrac12kA^2$.

notes.heading: Power
notes.body_md:
- Average power $P=W/t$; instantaneous power $P=\vec F\cdot\vec v$.
- SI unit watt (1 W = 1 J/s); 1 horsepower is about 746 W; 1 kWh = $3.6\times10^6$ J.
- A vehicle at constant power: $F=P/v$, so the pulling force falls as speed rises.
- Maximum speed occurs when driving force equals resistive force.

notes.heading: Collisions
notes.body_md:
- Momentum is conserved in every collision (isolated system).
- Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved. Inelastic: some kinetic energy is lost. Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick together, maximum loss.
- Coefficient of restitution $e=\dfrac{\text{speed of separation}}{\text{speed of approach}}$; $e=1$ elastic, $e=0$ perfectly inelastic.
- In a 1-D elastic collision of equal masses the velocities are exchanged.
- A ball dropped from $h_1$ rebounding to $h_2$ has $e=\sqrt{h_2/h_1}$.

pyqs.question: Prove the work-energy theorem for a constant force acting along a line. A 0.2 kg ball dropped from 5 m rebounds to 3.2 m. Find the coefficient of restitution and the mechanical energy lost in the bounce.
pyqs.solution_md:
For constant $a$: $v^2-u^2=2as$. Multiply by $m/2$: $\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mu^2=mas=Fs=W$. Hence $W_{net}=K_f-K_i$.

Ball: impact speed $v_1=\sqrt{2g(5)}$, rebound speed $v_2=\sqrt{2g(3.2)}$.
$e=v_2/v_1=\sqrt{3.2/5}=0.8$.

Energy lost $=mg(h_1-h_2)=0.2\times9.8\times1.8=3.53$ J.

chapters.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

notes.heading: Rigid bodies and types of motion
notes.body_md:
- A rigid body keeps fixed distances between its particles.
- Pure translation: all particles have the same velocity. Pure rotation about a fixed axis: every particle moves in a circle with the same angular velocity.
- Rolling is a combination of translation of the centre of mass and rotation about it.

notes.heading: Centre of mass
notes.body_md:
- For particles: $\vec R=\dfrac{\sum m_i\vec r_i}{\sum m_i}$.
- The centre of mass of a symmetric uniform body lies at its geometric centre (it may lie outside the body, as for a ring).
- Motion of the centre of mass: $M\vec a_{cm}=\vec F_{ext}$; internal forces do not affect it.
- If the net external force is zero, the centre of mass moves with constant velocity (an exploding shell's CM keeps following the original path).

notes.heading: Angular velocity, angular acceleration and kinematics
notes.body_md:
- $\omega=d\theta/dt$, $\alpha=d\omega/dt$; linear speed $v=r\omega$, tangential acceleration $a_t=r\alpha$.
- For constant $\alpha$: $\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t$, $\theta=\omega_0t+\tfrac12\alpha t^2$, $\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha\theta$.
- These mirror the linear equations with $x\to\theta$, $v\to\omega$, $a\to\alpha$.

notes.heading: Torque and angular momentum
notes.body_md:
- Torque $\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F$, magnitude $rF\sin\theta$ (force times perpendicular distance from the axis).
- Angular momentum $\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p$; for a rigid body about its axis $L=I\omega$.
- Rotational form of the second law: $\tau=\dfrac{dL}{dt}=I\alpha$.
- Equilibrium of a rigid body needs zero net force and zero net torque.

notes.heading: Moment of inertia
notes.body_md:
- $I=\sum m_ir_i^2$; it depends on mass, its distribution, and the axis.
- Ring (axis through centre, perpendicular): $MR^2$. Disc: $\tfrac12MR^2$. Solid sphere (diameter): $\tfrac25MR^2$. Hollow sphere: $\tfrac23MR^2$.
- Rod about centre perpendicular: $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$; about end: $\tfrac13ML^2$.
- Radius of gyration $k$: $I=Mk^2$.

notes.heading: Theorems of parallel and perpendicular axes
notes.body_md:
- Parallel axes: $I=I_{cm}+Md^2$, where $d$ is the distance between the parallel axes.
- Perpendicular axes (planar bodies only): $I_z=I_x+I_y$.
- The parallel axes theorem gives the smallest moment of inertia for the axis through the centre of mass.
- Example: disc about a diameter $=\tfrac14MR^2$ (using the perpendicular axes theorem).

notes.heading: Conservation of angular momentum and rotational energy
notes.body_md:
- If net external torque is zero, $L=I\omega$ is constant. A skater spins faster on pulling arms in because $I$ decreases.
- Rotational kinetic energy $\tfrac12I\omega^2$; power $P=\tau\omega$; work $W=\tau\theta$.
- Note that kinetic energy changes when $I$ changes even though $L$ is conserved (work is done by the skater).

notes.heading: Rolling motion
notes.body_md:
- Rolling without slipping: $v_{cm}=R\omega$; the contact point is momentarily at rest.
- Total kinetic energy $=\tfrac12Mv^2\left(1+\dfrac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$.
- Acceleration down an incline $a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2}$; bodies with smaller $k^2/R^2$ reach the bottom first (sphere before disc before ring).
- Friction at the contact point is static and does no work in pure rolling.

pyqs.question: Define torque. A force of 10 N acts perpendicular to a spanner 0.3 m long. Find the torque.
pyqs.solution_md: Torque is the turning effect of a force, $\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F$. Here $\tau=rF\sin90^\circ=0.3\times10=3$ N m.

pyqs.question: A 2 kg mass is at $x=0$ and a 3 kg mass is at $x=5$ m. Find the position of their centre of mass.
A skater spinning at 2 rad/s with moment of inertia 4 kg m$^2$ pulls her arms in so that $I$ becomes 2 kg m$^2$. Find the new angular speed and the initial and final kinetic energies.
pyqs.solution_md:
$L$ conserved: $4\times2=2\omega\Rightarrow\omega=4$ rad/s.
$K_i=\tfrac12(4)(2)^2=8$ J; $K_f=\tfrac12(2)(4)^2=16$ J.
The extra 8 J comes from work done by the skater's muscles.

pyqs.question: State and prove the theorem of parallel axes for a rigid body. Use it to find the moment of inertia of a 3 kg, 2 m uniform rod about an axis through one end perpendicular to the rod.
pyqs.answer: I = I_cm + M d^2; 4 kg m^2
pyqs.solution_md:
Let the axis through the centre of mass be CM, and a parallel axis be at distance $d$. For a particle of mass $m$ at perpendicular distance $r$ from the CM axis, its distance from the parallel axis is $r'$ with $r'^2=r^2+d^2+2\vec r\cdot\vec d$.

$I=\sum m r'^2=\sum mr^2+d^2\sum m+2\vec d\cdot\sum m\vec r$.

The last sum is zero because $\sum m\vec r=0$ about the centre of mass. Hence $I=I_{cm}+Md^2$.

Rod: $I_{cm}=\tfrac{1}{12}(3)(2)^2=1$ kg m$^2$; $d=1$ m. $I=1+3(1)^2=4$ kg m$^2$ (agrees with $\tfrac13ML^2$).

notes.heading: Kepler's laws of planetary motion
notes.body_md:
- Law of orbits: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
- Law of areas: the line joining the Sun and a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times (conservation of angular momentum), so a planet moves faster when nearer the Sun.
- Law of periods: $T^2\propto a^3$, where $a$ is the semi-major axis.

notes.heading: Universal law of gravitation
notes.body_md:
- Every pair of point masses attracts with force $F=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ along the line joining them.
- $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$/kg$^2$; it is a universal constant.
- Gravity is always attractive, acts at a distance and obeys the third law.
- For spherical bodies, the mass can be taken to be concentrated at the centre (shell theorem).

notes.heading: Acceleration due to gravity
notes.body_md:
- At the surface, $g=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ and the mass of the Earth follows from $M=gR^2/G$.
- Height $h\ll R$: $g_h\approx g\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$; exact $g_h=g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$.
- Depth $d$: $g_d=g\left(1-\dfrac{d}{R}\right)$, zero at the centre.
- Rotation and the Earth's shape make $g$ vary with latitude: minimum at the equator, maximum at the poles.

notes.heading: Gravitational potential energy
notes.body_md:
- Taking $U=0$ at infinity, the potential energy of two masses is $U=-\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}$.
- Gravitational potential $V=-\dfrac{GM}{r}$ (energy per unit mass).
- Near the surface, $mgh$ is the change of $U$ for small heights.
- Force is the negative gradient of potential energy: $F=-dU/dr$.

notes.heading: Escape speed
notes.body_md:
- Minimum speed needed to leave the Earth's gravity without further propulsion.
- $v_e=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}=\sqrt{2gR}\approx11.2$ km/s for Earth.
- It does not depend on the mass or direction of the projectile.
- $v_e=\sqrt2\,v_o$, where $v_o$ is the orbital speed just above the surface.
- For the Moon $v_e\approx2.4$ km/s, so it has no atmosphere.

notes.heading: Earth satellites
notes.body_md:
- Orbital speed at radius $r$: $v_o=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ (about 7.9 km/s near the surface).
- Time period $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM}}$; about 84 minutes near the surface.
- A geostationary satellite has $T=24$ h, orbits in the equatorial plane at about 36,000 km above the surface (radius about 42,400 km).
- A polar satellite passes over the poles and scans the whole Earth over time.

notes.heading: Energy of an orbiting satellite
notes.body_md:
- $K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, total $E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.
- Total energy is negative, which means the satellite is bound; binding energy is $+GMm/2r$.
- Moving to a higher orbit increases the total energy (less negative) but decreases the speed.
- Weightlessness in an orbit: the satellite and its contents are in free fall with the same acceleration.

notes.heading: Elasticity and plasticity
notes.body_md:
- Elasticity is the tendency of a body to regain its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed.
- Plasticity is the tendency to retain the deformation (putty, lead).
- Steel is more elastic than rubber, because for the same strain it develops a larger restoring stress.

notes.heading: Stress and strain
notes.body_md:
- Stress = restoring force per unit area, $\sigma=F/A$ (N/m$^2$ = Pa); dimension $ML^{-1}T^{-2}$.
- Types: longitudinal (tensile or compressive), shear (tangential), hydraulic (uniform pressure).
- Strain = fractional deformation, dimensionless: longitudinal $\Delta L/L$, shear $\theta=\Delta x/L$, volume $\Delta V/V$.

notes.heading: Hooke's law and the stress-strain curve
notes.body_md:
- Within the proportional limit, stress is proportional to strain; the ratio is the modulus of elasticity.
- Curve: proportional region, elastic limit, yield point, plastic region, ultimate tensile strength, fracture.
- Materials that fracture soon after the elastic limit are brittle; those with a long plastic region are ductile.
- Elastomers (rubber) show large strain with no proper proportionality and a hysteresis loop.

notes.heading: Young's modulus
notes.body_md:
- $Y=\dfrac{\text{longitudinal stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}=\dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$.
- It depends only on the material; steel $\approx2\times10^{11}$ Pa, copper $\approx1.1\times10^{11}$ Pa, aluminium $\approx7\times10^{10}$ Pa.
- Extension of a wire: $\Delta L\propto FL/(r^2Y)$; a wire acts like a spring of constant $k=YA/L$.
- The same force stretches a thinner or longer wire more.

notes.heading: Shear modulus and bulk modulus
notes.body_md:
- Shear modulus $G=\dfrac{F/A}{\theta}$ where $\theta$ is the angle of shear; liquids and gases have $G=0$.
- Bulk modulus $B=-\dfrac{p}{\Delta V/V}$; the negative sign shows that volume decreases as pressure increases.
- Compressibility $=1/B$.
- Solids have a high $B$; gases are the most compressible.

notes.heading: Poisson's ratio
notes.body_md:
- When a wire is stretched it becomes thinner. Poisson's ratio $\sigma=\dfrac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}$ in magnitude.
- It is a pure number; its theoretical limits are $-1$ and $0.5$, and for most materials $0$ to $0.5$.
- Lateral strain is $\Delta d/d$ (change in diameter over original diameter).

notes.heading: Elastic potential energy
notes.body_md:
- Work done in stretching a wire is stored as elastic potential energy: $U=\tfrac12F\,\Delta L=\tfrac12k(\Delta L)^2$.
- Energy per unit volume $u=\tfrac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2Y}=\tfrac12Y\varepsilon^2$.
- Energy lost in rubber appears as heat (hysteresis), making it useful in shock absorbers.

notes.heading: Applications of elastic behaviour
notes.body_md:
- Cranes use steel ropes with a safe load far below the breaking stress.
- Bridges and beams are made with an I-shaped cross section to resist bending with less material.
- A beam of length $l$, breadth $b$ and depth $d$ has deflection proportional to $l^3/(bd^3Y)$, so depth matters most.
- Mountains have a limited height because the base rock must withstand the weight above it.

pyqs.question: The SI unit of Young's modulus is:
pyqs.solution_md: $Y$ = stress/strain, and strain is dimensionless, so its unit is that of stress, N/m$^2$ (pascal).

pyqs.question: State Hooke's law and define the elastic limit.
pyqs.answer: Stress is proportional to strain within the elastic limit.
pyqs.solution_md:
Hooke's law: within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain; the constant is the modulus of elasticity.
Elastic limit: the maximum stress up to which the body fully regains its original dimensions on removing the load.

pyqs.question: A steel wire of length 2 m and diameter 1 mm carries a 10 kg load. Find the extension ($Y=2\times10^{11}$ Pa, $g=9.8$ m/s$^2$).
Two wires of the same material have lengths in the ratio 1 : 2 and radii in the ratio 2 : 1. They carry the same load. Find the ratio of their extensions.
Draw and explain the stress-strain curve for a ductile metal wire. Water has bulk modulus $2.2\times10^{9}$ Pa; find the fractional compression when the pressure increases by $2\times10^{7}$ Pa.
pyqs.solution_md:
Curve (strain on x-axis, stress on y-axis):
- OA: straight line, Hooke's law valid; A is the proportional limit.
- AB: stress and strain no longer proportional but the wire still returns to its original length; B is the elastic limit.
- Beyond B: the wire shows permanent set; C is the yield point where strain rises rapidly.
- CD: plastic region; D is the ultimate tensile strength (maximum stress).
- DE: the wire thins (necking) and breaks at E (fracture point).

Numerical: $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=\dfrac{\Delta p}{B}=\dfrac{2\times10^7}{2.2\times10^9}=9.1\times10^{-3}$, i.e. 0.91%.

pyqs.question: A wire is stressed to $4\times10^{7}$ Pa. If $Y=2\times10^{11}$ Pa, the elastic energy stored per unit volume is:
A wire of length 1 m and cross-section $10^{-6}$ m$^2$ has $Y=2\times10^{11}$ Pa. What tension is needed to stretch it by 1 mm?
A wire of length $L$ extends by $\Delta L$ under a force $F$. If the same wire is cut to half its length and the same force is applied, the extension is:
pyqs.solution_md: $\Delta L=FL/AY\propto L$. Halving the length halves the extension: $\Delta L/2$.

pyqs.question: A cube of side 10 cm is subjected to a tangential force so that its top face is displaced 0.5 mm relative to the bottom. If $G=8\times10^{10}$ Pa, find the force.
pyqs.solution_md:
Shear angle $\theta=\Delta x/L=5\times10^{-4}/0.1=5\times10^{-3}$.
Area $=0.01$ m$^2$.
$F=GA\theta=8\times10^{10}\times0.01\times5\times10^{-3}=4\times10^{6}$ N.

pyqs.question:
Assertion (A): Steel is more elastic than rubber.
Reason (R): Steel has a larger Young's modulus than rubber.
options: (A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
(B) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
(C) A is true but R is false
(D) A is false but R is true
pyqs.solution_md: Elasticity is judged by the restoring stress for a given strain; a larger $Y$ means a larger restoring stress per unit strain, so R explains A.

notes.heading: Pressure in a fluid
notes.body_md:
- Pressure $p=F/A$ (pascal, Pa); atmospheric pressure is about $1.013\times10^5$ Pa.
- Pressure at depth $h$: $p=p_0+\rho gh$; gauge pressure is $\rho gh$.
- Pressure depends on depth, not on the shape of the container (hydrostatic paradox).
- Pressure is a scalar, acting equally in all directions at a point.
- Barometer: the height of a mercury column (76 cm) balances atmospheric pressure.

notes.heading: Pascal's law and hydraulic machines
notes.body_md:
- A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of it.
- Hydraulic lift: $F_2=F_1\dfrac{A_2}{A_1}$, giving a mechanical advantage.
- Energy is conserved: the smaller piston moves a larger distance.
- Applications: hydraulic jacks, brakes, presses.

notes.heading: Buoyancy and Archimedes' principle
notes.body_md:
- A body in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
- A body floats if its average density is less than the fluid's; the submerged fraction is $\rho_{body}/\rho_{fluid}$.
- Apparent weight in a fluid = true weight - buoyant force.
- A floating body is in stable equilibrium when its centre of gravity lies below the centre of buoyancy (or the metacentre is above the C.G.).

notes.heading: Streamline flow, continuity and Bernoulli's principle
notes.body_md:
- Streamline (steady) flow: velocity at a point is constant; streamlines never cross.
- Equation of continuity (incompressible): $A_1v_1=A_2v_2$.
- Bernoulli: $p+\tfrac12\rho v^2+\rho gh=$ constant along a streamline (non-viscous, incompressible, steady flow).
- Where speed is high, pressure is low.
- Applications: Torricelli's law $v=\sqrt{2gh}$, Venturi meter, atomiser, lift on an aerofoil, why ships moving close attract.

notes.heading: Viscosity
notes.body_md:
- Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid opposing relative motion between layers: $F=\eta A\dfrac{dv}{dx}$.
- Unit of $\eta$: pascal second (Pa s); poise = 0.1 Pa s.
- Viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature; that of gases increases.
- Stokes' law: drag on a sphere $F=6\pi\eta rv$.
- Terminal velocity: $v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}$, where $\sigma$ is the density of the fluid.

notes.heading: Reynolds number and turbulence
notes.body_md:
- $Re=\dfrac{\rho vd}{\eta}$ decides flow type: below about 1000 flow is laminar; above about 2000 it becomes turbulent.
- Turbulent flow is irregular, with eddies, and has higher resistance.
- Streamlined shapes delay turbulence in vehicles and aircraft.

notes.heading: Surface tension
notes.body_md:
- Surface tension $S=F/l$, the force per unit length on a line drawn in the surface (N/m); it is also surface energy per unit area (J/m$^2$).
- It arises from unbalanced cohesive forces on surface molecules, and decreases as temperature rises or with detergents.
- Work to increase the area of a surface: $W=S\,\Delta A$.
- Droplets and bubbles tend to be spherical to minimise area.

notes.heading: Excess pressure, angle of contact and capillarity
notes.body_md:
- Excess pressure inside a liquid drop $=\dfrac{2S}{r}$; inside a soap bubble (two surfaces) $=\dfrac{4S}{r}$.
- Angle of contact is acute for wetting liquids (water on glass) and obtuse for non-wetting ones (mercury on glass).
- Capillary rise: $h=\dfrac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho gr}$; mercury is depressed.
- Practical examples: oil rising in a wick, ink absorbed by blotting paper.

notes.heading: Temperature and heat
notes.body_md:
- Temperature measures the degree of hotness; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference (SI unit joule; 1 cal = 4.186 J).
- Scales: $\dfrac{C}{5}=\dfrac{F-32}{9}=\dfrac{K-273.15}{5}$.
- Celsius and Fahrenheit readings coincide at $-40$.
- Ideal gas thermometer: $T\propto p$ at constant volume; absolute zero is $0$ K ($-273.15^\circ$C).

notes.heading: Thermal expansion
notes.body_md:
- Linear: $\Delta L=\alpha L\,\Delta T$; area: $\Delta A=\beta A\,\Delta T$ with $\beta=2\alpha$; volume: $\Delta V=\gamma V\,\Delta T$ with $\gamma=3\alpha$.
- Liquids expand more than solids; the apparent expansion in a vessel is $\gamma_{app}=\gamma_{liquid}-\gamma_{vessel}$.
- Water contracts from $0^\circ$C to $4^\circ$C (anomalous expansion) and has maximum density at $4^\circ$C, so lakes freeze from the top.
- A rod prevented from expanding develops thermal stress $=Y\alpha\Delta T$.

notes.heading: Specific heat and calorimetry
notes.body_md:
- Heat required $Q=mc\,\Delta T$; heat capacity $C=mc$; molar specific heat is per mole.
- Water has a high specific heat $\approx4200$ J/(kg K), so it is a good coolant and moderates climate.
- Calorimetry principle: heat lost by hot bodies = heat gained by cold bodies (no losses).
- Include the calorimeter's water equivalent if it is given.

notes.heading: Change of state and latent heat
notes.body_md:
- During a change of state the temperature stays constant while heat is absorbed or released: $Q=mL$.
- Latent heat of fusion of ice $=3.36\times10^5$ J/kg; of vaporisation of water $=2.26\times10^6$ J/kg.
- The heating curve of ice has sloped parts (single phase) and flat parts (phase change).
- Boiling point rises with pressure; melting point of ice falls slightly with pressure (regelation).
- Sublimation: solid to vapour directly (dry ice, camphor).

notes.heading: Heat transfer: conduction
notes.body_md:
- Conduction needs a material medium and no bulk motion of matter.
- Steady state rate: $H=\dfrac{Q}{t}=KA\dfrac{T_1-T_2}{L}$, where $K$ is the thermal conductivity (W/(m K)).
- Thermal resistance $R=\dfrac{L}{KA}$; resistances add in series and conductances add in parallel.
- For slabs in series, the same heat flows through each, which fixes the interface temperature.

notes.heading: Heat transfer: convection and radiation
notes.body_md:
- Convection: heat transfer by actual movement of a fluid (sea breeze, boiling water, ocean currents).
- Radiation: transfer by electromagnetic waves, needing no medium (sunlight).
- Good absorbers are good emitters; a perfect black body absorbs all radiation.
- Stefan-Boltzmann law: power radiated $P=\sigma AeT^4$.

notes.heading: Newton's law of cooling
notes.body_md:
- The rate of fall of temperature is proportional to the excess temperature over the surroundings for small differences: $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_s)$.
- Solution: $T-T_s=(T_0-T_s)e^{-kt}$.
- Approximation for short intervals: $\dfrac{T_1-T_2}{t}=k\left(\dfrac{T_1+T_2}{2}-T_s\right)$.
- Cooling curve is exponential, dropping fast at first and then slowing.

50 g of ice at 0 C is dropped into 200 g of water at 40 C. Find the final temperature ($L_f=3.36\times10^5$ J/kg, $c_w=4200$ J/(kg K); ignore losses).
pyqs.solution_md:
Heat released by water cooling to 0 C: $0.2\times4200\times40=33600$ J.
Heat to melt ice: $0.05\times3.36\times10^5=16800$ J (so all ice melts).
Remaining $16800$ J heats $0.25$ kg: $\Delta T=\dfrac{16800}{0.25\times4200}=16$ C.

pyqs.question: Derive the interface temperature for two slabs of equal area and thickness and conductivities $2K$ and $K$ in contact, with outer faces at 100 C and 0 C. State the formula for conduction and define thermal resistance.
pyqs.solution_md:
Conduction: $H=KA(T_1-T_2)/L$; thermal resistance $R=L/KA$ (series resistances add).

In steady state, the same $H$ flows through both slabs. Let the interface be at $T$:
$\dfrac{2KA(100-T)}{d}=\dfrac{KA(T-0)}{d}\Rightarrow2(100-T)=T\Rightarrow T=\dfrac{200}{3}=66.7$ C.

pyqs.question: A body cools from 80 C to 60 C in 10 min in surroundings at 20 C. Using Newton's law of cooling, the time it takes to cool from 60 C to 40 C is closest to:
pyqs.solution_md:
$T-T_s\propto e^{-kt}$: $\ln\dfrac{60}{40}=10k\Rightarrow k=0.0405$ min$^{-1}$.
For 60 C to 40 C: $t=\dfrac1k\ln\dfrac{40}{20}=\dfrac{0.693}{0.0405}\approx17$ min.

pyqs.solution_md:
Heat gained by water $=1\times4200\times5=21000$ J.
Heat lost by metal $=0.5\,c\,(100-25)=37.5\,c$.
$c=21000/37.5=560$ J/(kg K).

Assertion (A): A metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon at the same room temperature.
Reason (R): Metals have a higher thermal conductivity than wood.

(B) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
(C) A is true but R is false

notes.heading: Thermal equilibrium and zeroth law
notes.body_md:
- Two systems in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature.
- Zeroth law: if A and B are each in equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other; this makes thermometry possible.
- State variables (P, V, T, U) describe the state of a system; heat and work are path functions, not state functions.

notes.heading: Heat, internal energy and work
notes.body_md:
- Internal energy $U$ is the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies; for an ideal gas it depends only on temperature.
- Work done by a gas $W=\int P\,dV$, the area under the P-V curve; positive in expansion, negative in compression.
- Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.

notes.heading: First law of thermodynamics
notes.body_md:
- $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W$: heat supplied goes into raising internal energy and doing work.
- Sign convention: $Q>0$ heat absorbed by the gas; $W>0$ work done by the gas.
- It is the law of conservation of energy for thermal systems.
- Over a complete cycle $\Delta U=0$, so net heat equals net work, the area enclosed in the P-V diagram.

notes.heading: Specific heats of a gas
notes.body_md:
- $C_v$: molar specific heat at constant volume, $\Delta U=nC_v\Delta T$ for any process of an ideal gas.
- $C_p$: at constant pressure; $C_p-C_v=R$ (Mayer's relation); $\gamma=C_p/C_v$.
- Monatomic gas: $C_v=\tfrac32R$, $\gamma=\tfrac53$. Diatomic (rigid): $C_v=\tfrac52R$, $\gamma=\tfrac75$.
- $C_p>C_v$ because at constant pressure some heat goes into expansion work.

notes.heading: Thermodynamic processes
notes.body_md:
- Isothermal ($T$ constant): $PV=$ constant, $\Delta U=0$, $Q=W=nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$.
- Adiabatic ($Q=0$): $PV^\gamma=$ constant, $TV^{\gamma-1}=$ constant, $W=\dfrac{nR(T_1-T_2)}{\gamma-1}$.
- Isochoric ($V$ constant): $W=0$, $Q=\Delta U=nC_v\Delta T$.
- Isobaric ($P$ constant): $W=P\Delta V$, $Q=nC_p\Delta T$.
- On a P-V diagram an adiabat is steeper than an isotherm.

notes.heading: Second law of thermodynamics
notes.body_md:
- Kelvin-Planck: no engine can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work in a cycle.
- Clausius: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder to a hotter body without external work.
- Hence no heat engine has 100% efficiency and no refrigerator works without work input.
- Spontaneous processes in nature are irreversible.

notes.heading: Heat engines and Carnot cycle
notes.body_md:
- Efficiency $\eta=\dfrac{W}{Q_1}=1-\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1}$.
- Carnot cycle: two isothermal and two adiabatic steps, all reversible.
- Carnot engine efficiency $\eta=1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$ (temperatures in kelvin) is the maximum possible between two reservoirs; it depends only on the temperatures.
- Efficiency rises by raising the source temperature or lowering the sink temperature.

notes.heading: Refrigerators and reversibility
notes.body_md:
- A refrigerator takes heat $Q_2$ from a cold space, receives work $W$, and rejects $Q_1=Q_2+W$ to the surroundings.
- Coefficient of performance $\text{COP}=\dfrac{Q_2}{W}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$ for a reversible refrigerator.
- A process is reversible only if it is quasi-static and free of dissipative effects such as friction.
- Real processes are irreversible.

Heat 1 mole at constant volume: $\Delta Q=C_v\Delta T=\Delta U$.
Heat 1 mole at constant pressure: $C_p\Delta T=\Delta U+P\Delta V$. Since $\Delta U=C_v\Delta T$ (depends only on $T$) and $P\Delta V=R\Delta T$ from $PV=RT$:
$C_p\Delta T=C_v\Delta T+R\Delta T\Rightarrow C_p-C_v=R$.

Numerical: $C_v=\tfrac32R$; $\Delta U=nC_v\Delta T=2\times1.5\times8.314\times100=2494$ J $\approx2.49$ kJ (all of it is the heat supplied since $W=0$).

Assertion (A): The efficiency of a heat engine can never be 100%.

notes.heading: Molecular nature of matter and gas laws
notes.body_md:
- Matter is made of molecules in constant motion; in a gas they are far apart with negligible forces except during collisions.
- Boyle's law: $PV=$ const at constant $T$. Charles' law: $V/T=$ const at constant $P$. Gay-Lussac: $P/T=$ const at constant $V$.
- Combined: $PV=nRT=NkT$, with $R=8.314$ J/(mol K), $k=1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K, $N_A=6.02\times10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$.
- Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same $T$ and $P$ contain equal numbers of molecules.

notes.heading: Assumptions of the kinetic theory
notes.body_md:
- A gas contains a very large number of identical, tiny molecules in random motion.
- The size of molecules is negligible compared with the separation between them.
- No forces act except during elastic collisions with each other and the walls.
- Collision time is negligible compared with the time between collisions.
- Molecules obey Newton's laws and move in straight lines between collisions.

notes.heading: Pressure of an ideal gas
notes.body_md:
- Pressure arises from the momentum transferred to the walls by molecular collisions.
- $P=\tfrac13\dfrac{N}{V}m\overline{v^2}=\tfrac13\rho\overline{v^2}$.
- Equivalently $P=\tfrac23\dfrac NV\left(\tfrac12m\overline{v^2}\right)$, so pressure is two-thirds of the translational energy per unit volume.
- Combining with $PV=NkT$ gives the kinetic interpretation of temperature.

notes.heading: Kinetic interpretation of temperature
notes.body_md:
- Average translational kinetic energy per molecule $=\tfrac32kT$; it depends only on temperature.
- $v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3kT}{m}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$, with $M$ the molar mass.
- Most probable speed $=\sqrt{2kT/m}$ and mean speed $=\sqrt{8kT/\pi m}$; $v_{mp}<\bar v<v_{rms}$.
- At the same temperature lighter molecules move faster (hydrogen faster than oxygen).
- Dalton's law: total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of partial pressures.

notes.heading: Degrees of freedom and equipartition of energy
notes.body_md:
- Degrees of freedom $f$ are independent ways a molecule can store energy: monatomic 3; diatomic 5 at ordinary temperatures (3 translational + 2 rotational), plus 2 vibrational at high temperature.
- Law of equipartition: each quadratic degree of freedom has average energy $\tfrac12kT$ per molecule.
- Internal energy of $n$ moles: $U=\tfrac f2nRT$.
- Vibrational modes carry $kT$ each (kinetic and potential).

notes.heading: Specific heat capacities of gases
notes.body_md:
- $C_v=\tfrac f2R$ and $C_p=\left(\tfrac f2+1\right)R$, hence $\gamma=1+\dfrac2f$.
- Monatomic: $C_v=\tfrac32R$, $\gamma=1.67$. Diatomic (rigid): $C_v=\tfrac52R$, $\gamma=1.40$. Non-linear polyatomic: $f=6$.
- For a mixture, $C_v^{mix}=\dfrac{n_1C_{v1}+n_2C_{v2}}{n_1+n_2}$.
- Specific heat of solids at room temperature: $3R$ (Dulong-Petit law), which includes both kinetic and potential energy of vibration.

notes.heading: Mean free path
notes.body_md:
- Mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions: $\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2n}$.
- Here $d$ is the molecular diameter and $n=N/V$ is the number density.
- $\lambda$ decreases with higher pressure and larger molecular size; at room temperature and 1 atm it is of order $10^{-7}$ m, which is about a thousand times the molecular diameter.
- Equivalent form: $\lambda=\dfrac{kT}{\sqrt2\pi d^2P}$.

pyqs.question: Derive the expression $P=\tfrac13\rho\overline{v^2}$ for the pressure of an ideal gas. A gas of density 1.2 kg/m$^3$ has an rms speed of 500 m/s; find its pressure.
pyqs.solution_md:
Consider a cubical box of side $L$. A molecule with velocity component $v_x$ hits a wall and rebounds, changing its momentum by $2mv_x$. It strikes the same wall every $2L/v_x$.

Force from one molecule $=\dfrac{2mv_x}{2L/v_x}=\dfrac{mv_x^2}{L}$.

For $N$ molecules, $F=\dfrac{m}{L}\sum v_x^2=\dfrac{mN\overline{v_x^2}}{L}$. By symmetry $\overline{v_x^2}=\tfrac13\overline{v^2}$.

Pressure $P=\dfrac{F}{L^2}=\dfrac13\dfrac{N}{V}m\overline{v^2}=\tfrac13\rho\overline{v^2}$.

Numerical: $P=\tfrac13(1.2)(500)^2=1.0\times10^5$ Pa.

notes.heading: Periodic and oscillatory motion
notes.body_md:
- Periodic motion repeats at regular intervals; oscillatory motion is back-and-forth about a mean position.
- Period $T$ is the time for one cycle; frequency $\nu=1/T$ (hertz); angular frequency $\omega=2\pi\nu=2\pi/T$.
- Every oscillation is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory (e.g. uniform circular motion).

notes.heading: Simple harmonic motion
notes.body_md:
- SHM: the restoring force (or acceleration) is proportional to displacement and directed toward the mean position, $F=-kx$, $a=-\omega^2x$.
- Displacement $x=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ where $A$ is amplitude and $\phi$ the initial phase.
- Projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter is SHM (reference circle).
- Period does not depend on amplitude for ideal SHM.

notes.heading: Velocity and acceleration in SHM
notes.body_md:
- $v=-A\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi)=\pm\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$.
- Maximum speed $A\omega$ occurs at the mean position; speed is zero at the extremes.
- $a=-\omega^2x$, maximum $A\omega^2$ at the extremes and zero at the mean position.
- Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$ in phase, and acceleration is opposite in phase to displacement.

notes.heading: Energy in SHM
notes.body_md:
- $K=\tfrac12m\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$ and $U=\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2=\tfrac12kx^2$.
- Total energy $E=\tfrac12kA^2=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2$, constant when there is no damping.
- Kinetic and potential energies each oscillate at twice the frequency of the motion; their averages over a cycle are each $E/2$.
- $K=U$ at $x=\pm A/\sqrt2$.

notes.heading: Spring-mass system
notes.body_md:
- $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$, $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.
- For a vertical spring, the equilibrium shifts by $mg/k$ but the period is unchanged: $T=2\pi\sqrt{x_0/g}$ where $x_0$ is the static extension.
- Parallel springs: $k_{eq}=k_1+k_2$. Series springs: $\dfrac{1}{k_{eq}}=\dfrac1{k_1}+\dfrac1{k_2}$.
- Cutting a spring into $n$ equal pieces increases each piece's spring constant by a factor of $n$.

notes.heading: Simple pendulum
notes.body_md:
- For small angles (less than about $10^\circ$), $T=2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, independent of the mass and amplitude.
- A seconds pendulum has $T=2$ s, which needs $l\approx0.99$ m at the Earth's surface.
- $T$ increases on hills or on the Moon (smaller $g$), and increases with temperature as $l$ increases.
- In a lift accelerating upward $g_{eff}=g+a$ and the period decreases; in free fall it becomes infinite.

notes.heading: Phase and phase difference
notes.body_md:
- Phase $\omega t+\phi$ gives the state of motion at time $t$.
- Two SHMs of the same frequency differ by phase difference $\Delta\phi$; $0$ means in phase, $\pi$ means opposite phase.
- Initial phase is fixed by the initial conditions: at $t=0$ with $x=A$, $\phi=0$.
- $\sin(\omega t)$ equals $\cos(\omega t-\pi/2)$, which shifts the phase.

pyqs.question: Show that the total energy of a particle in SHM is $\tfrac12kA^2$ and is independent of time. A mass on a spring with $k=100$ N/m has amplitude 0.2 m; find its kinetic and potential energy at $x=0.1$ m.
pyqs.answer: E = 2 J; PE = 0.5 J; KE = 1.5 J
pyqs.solution_md:
$x=A\cos\omega t$, $v=-A\omega\sin\omega t$, $k=m\omega^2$.

$U=\tfrac12kx^2=\tfrac12kA^2\cos^2\omega t$; $K=\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12kA^2\sin^2\omega t$.

$E=K+U=\tfrac12kA^2(\sin^2+\cos^2)=\tfrac12kA^2$, constant.

Numerical: $E=\tfrac12(100)(0.04)=2$ J; $U=\tfrac12(100)(0.01)=0.5$ J; $K=E-U=1.5$ J.

notes.heading: Wave motion and types of waves
notes.body_md:
- A wave transfers energy and momentum without bulk transport of matter.
- Transverse waves: particle motion perpendicular to propagation (waves on a string, light); they travel in solids and on liquid surfaces.
- Longitudinal waves: particle motion parallel to propagation (sound), forming compressions and rarefactions; they travel in all media.
- Mechanical waves need a medium; electromagnetic waves do not.

notes.heading: Displacement relation of a progressive wave
notes.body_md:
- $y(x,t)=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)$ travels in the $+x$ direction; $\sin(kx+\omega t)$ travels in the $-x$ direction.
- Wave number $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$; angular frequency $\omega=2\pi\nu$; speed $v=\nu\lambda=\dfrac{\omega}{k}$.
- Phase difference between two points separated by $\Delta x$: $\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$.
- Particle velocity $\partial y/\partial t$ is different from wave speed.

notes.heading: Speed of waves
notes.body_md:
- Transverse wave on a string: $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ with $T$ the tension and $\mu$ the mass per unit length.
- Longitudinal wave in a solid rod: $v=\sqrt{Y/\rho}$; in a fluid: $v=\sqrt{B/\rho}$.
- Sound in a gas: Newton $v=\sqrt{P/\rho}$ (isothermal, gives wrong result); Laplace correction $v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$ (adiabatic, correct).
- Speed of sound in air $\propto\sqrt T$; about 332 m/s at $0^\circ$C and 343 m/s at $20^\circ$C; it does not depend on pressure at constant temperature.

notes.heading: Superposition, reflection and interference
notes.body_md:
- Principle of superposition: the net displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
- Reflection from a fixed (rigid) end inverts the pulse (phase change of $\pi$); reflection from a free end does not.
- Constructive interference: in-phase waves give amplitude $A_1+A_2$; destructive: out of phase give $|A_1-A_2|$.
- Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

notes.heading: Standing waves on strings
notes.body_md:
- Formed by superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) alternate, spaced $\lambda/2$.
- String fixed at both ends of length $L$: $\nu_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}$, $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ (all harmonics).
- The fundamental ($n=1$) has $\lambda=2L$; overtones are integer multiples.
- No energy is transported by a standing wave.

notes.heading: Standing waves in air columns
notes.body_md:
- Open pipe (both ends open): $\nu_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}$, all harmonics; antinodes at both ends.
- Closed pipe (one end closed): $\nu=\dfrac{(2n-1)v}{4L}$, only odd harmonics; node at the closed end and antinode at the open end.
- Fundamental of a closed pipe is half that of an open pipe of the same length.
- Resonance occurs when the air column length fits the driving frequency.

notes.heading: Beats
notes.body_md:
- Superposition of two waves of slightly different frequencies $
u_1,
u_2$ produces periodic variations in loudness.
- Beat frequency $=|
u_1-
u_2|$ (beats per second).
- Loading a tuning fork with wax lowers its frequency; filing raises it.
- Beats are used to tune musical instruments.

notes.heading: Doppler effect
notes.body_md:
- The observed frequency changes when the source or observer moves relative to the medium.
- $\nu'=\nu\left(\dfrac{v\pm v_o}{v\mp v_s}\right)$: use $+v_o$ when the observer moves towards the source and $-v_s$ in the denominator when the source moves towards the observer.
- Approach raises the frequency; recession lowers it.
- Only the component of velocity along the line joining source and observer matters.
